title: Al-Waliyy, the Protecting Friend
tomorrow: why does Dadi say alhamdulillah when it hurts?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Matin: unbreakable might, and small things kept up until Thursday. The line: firm. Then a question about one Name and two English words.

Somewhere in a phone's settings there's a list called trusted contacts: the people who can get you back into your account if you're locked out. Is that a friend, or a guardian? Usually both. Today's Name has the same problem in English. Al-Waliyy. Translations go back and forth between guardian, protector and friend, and the Arabic word holds all of them. So which one is it? Two readings, and each one has a real case. Let them both speak.

The first reading says guardian. In Arabic a wali is also the one who takes charge for someone: in Islamic law, the guardian who stands for a person is called their wali. And in Surah al-Baqarah, Allah is the wali of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light. That's not a feeling. That's a rescue. The best case for this side: friends can be fickle, but a guardian is on the hook for you, and doesn't wait to be asked. The second reading says friend. In Surah Yunus, Pickthall's words: "Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve." The Arabic there is awliya, the plural of wali. Later Muslims used that same word for people known to be near to God. The best case for this side: you thank a guardian politely, but you talk to a friend at two in the morning, and this Name invites the second kind of talk. Here's what's worth telling a friend tonight: the title of today's lesson, the Protecting Friend, refuses to choose. Protecting is the guardian. Friend is the nearness. Which half someone leans on can change with the night.

segments.voice: Find a scrap of paper and a pen. Write one line of thanks the way you'd text a close friend: short, plain, about one specific thing from this week. If you pray, it can be to Allah; it can also go to whoever has been on your side lately. Then hold the paper for the two minutes and let the line be enough.

segments.voice: Al-Waliyy. The Protecting Friend: a guardian who takes charge, and a friend who stays near, in one word.
Your line: friend. The one who takes charge of you and stays near. That's day fifteen twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah as Al-Waliyy in du'a and speak of the awliya, the friends of Allah, from Surah Yunus; in Islamic law a wali is also a guardian, as in marriage.

fork.setup: in your study circle, one person says Al-Waliyy should always be translated 'guardian'; another insists on 'friend'. you're asked to sum up fairly. what do you say?
options: guardian. 'friend' makes God sound too casual.
friend. 'guardian' makes God sound too distant.
both are in the word: a wali takes charge, and awliya are near.
fork.reveal: Surah al-Baqarah shows the wali rescuing, out of darkness into light; Surah Yunus calls those near Him awliya, friends. 'Protecting Friend' keeps both, and neither side has to lose.

original.note: Arabic: the Protecting Friend. its plural, awliya, names the friends of Allah in Surah Yunus.

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a buddy.
what it means: the one who takes charge of you and the one who is near you, both at once.
what a scholar hears: wali, plural awliya; 2:257 (out of darkness into light) beside 10:62 (no fear, no grief); the same word names a legal guardian.

chat.says: jordan skipped her own game to sit w dadi so i could take my chem test. 'thx' feels so tiny.
options: Tell her the exact thing she did and what it meant. Friends get plain, real thanks.
Get a big formal card. A favor that size deserves official gratitude.

chat.meaning: A wali is both guardian and friend, and a friend gets thanks that is close and specific, like a text, not a ceremony.
